source.title_on_document: When ChatGPT is gone: Creativity reverts and homogeneity persists

paper_design_summary: Sixty-one college students were randomly assigned to use ChatGPT 4.0 (n = 31) or to work alone (n = 30) in a seven-day lab experiment. Each day they did an alternative uses test (AUT) and a product problem-solving task; all worked without AI on Day 1 (baseline) and Day 7, the treatment group used ChatGPT on Days 2 to 6, and a Day 30 follow-up repeated one AUT without AI. Blind raters scored novelty, usefulness, flexibility, and expert ratings of the solutions, and SBERT cosine similarity, string matching, and UMAP density measures scored homogeneity across participants.

studies.label: Seven-day lab experiment with Day 30 follow-up (AUT and product problem-solving)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of ChatGPT 4.0 on the creative tasks of Days 2 to 6 versus completing the same tasks without ChatGPT
assignment.quote: After consenting to the study, they were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: ChatGPT use (the treatment group, n = 31) and no ChatGPT use (the control group, n = 30).

arms.name: ChatGPT (treatment, 'GPT' / 'Experimental')
arms.description: Given ChatGPT 4.0 to help finish both creative tasks on Days 2 to 6; no ChatGPT on Day 1, Day 7, and Day 30

arms.name: No ChatGPT (control)
arms.description: Completed the same two creative tasks by themselves on all days

participants.exclusions: None reported. Table 1 note gives N=61. The number who completed the Day 30 follow-up is not stated.
participants.who: Sixty-one college students (mean age 21.56, SD 2.62; 36 female) with 31 different majors from one university; p. 24 says undergraduates, graduates, and Ph.D. candidates
participants.quote: Sixty-one college students (Mage = 21.56 years, SD = 2.62) with 31 different majors from a university completed the lab experiment
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 11-12, Table 1 note (N=61); p. 24, Section 4.2

ai_tool.how_used: Treatment participants were provided ChatGPT 4.0 to help them finish the AUT and problem-solving tasks on Days 2 to 6 (p. 5). The paper does not describe prompts or restrictions.

task.description: Each day: Task 1, an alternative uses test (e.g., pen, brick; Day 30 uses a sponge), and Task 2, a high-complexity problem-solving task proposing new functions and solutions for a company product (e.g., VR glasses). Task order counterbalanced. Task 2 is idea_generation.
task.duration: Seven consecutive days plus a Day 30 follow-up; AUT limited to 3 minutes per day; Task 2 untimed

outcomes.name: Task 1 (AUT) novelty, Days 2 to 6 (ChatGPT available)

outcomes.measure_detail: Two blind raters (CAT) rated each extracted idea for novelty; participant novelty = sum of idea scores (ICC >= .90). Sum, not mean, so it also reflects number of ideas. Independent-samples t-tests (R) by day.

outcomes.name: Task 1 (AUT) semantic similarity across responses (SBERT), Days 2 to 6 (ChatGPT available)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean cosine similarity of SBERT sentence embeddings of responses, per group per day; higher = more homogeneous (direction coded on diversity, so sign reversed). Robustness variants: (a) string-matching 'redundancy' (repeated strings longer than two characters, Table 3); (b) UMAP density of SBERT embeddings: standard deviation, sum of eigenvalues, and ellipse area per group (Table 4a), where lower = less dispersed.

contrasts.reported: SBERT similarity Control vs GPT (Table 3): Day 2 0.39 vs 0.48; Day 3 0.32 vs 0.48; Day 4 0.3 vs 0.45; Day 5 0.48 vs 0.59; Day 6 0.38 vs 0.53 (Day 1 0.36 vs 0.35, n.s.). Text: 'the similarity of MC = [0.3, 0.48], the similarity of ME = [0.35, 59], ps <= .01'. String matching Control vs GPT: Day 2 2.73 vs 5.9; Day 3 3.17 vs 8.24; Day 4 3.33 vs 7.12; Day 5 3.4 vs 8.73; Day 6 3.13 vs 7.95; text 'MC = [3.13, 3.4] ... ME = [5.90, 8.73], ps <= .01'. Table 4a SD Control vs GPT: Day 2 0.40/0.33, Day 3 0.34/0.41, Day 4 0.37/0.32, Day 5 0.36/0.33, Day 6 0.37/0.32. Similarity higher for GPT = diversity lower.
contrasts.locator: p. 14, text; p. 15, text; p. 16, Table 3; p. 17, Table 4a; pp. 18-19, Figure 4a

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of SBERT sentence embeddings (plus string-matching redundancy and UMAP dispersion as variants)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SBERT (Reimers and Gurevych 2019); authors say 'we first trained the SBERT model'; checkpoint not named
diversity_detail.computed_over: Cosine similarity between pairs of answers; the paper does not state which pairs (all pairs within a condition-day or otherwise) or whether AUT ideas from the same participant are paired
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Not described. Text reports ps <= .01; Table 3 note says non-bold numbers are significant (p <= .001) but no cell is bold. No test named for similarity.
diversity_detail.notes: Table 4a dispersion is lower for GPT on Days 2, 4, 5, 6 but higher on Day 3 (SD 0.41 vs 0.34).

company_involvement.description: Coauthor Jihao Huang is affiliated with Beijing Yuxin Technology Company. No funding statement or role description appears in the document.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to ChatGPT 4.0 or no ChatGPT on AUT and product-idea tasks (p. 4); 61 people analyzed, 31 treatment and 30 control (p. 4; Table 1 note N=61); outcomes are blind-rater novelty, usefulness, and creativity scores and SBERT similarity of outputs (pp. 6, 13-16). The count is above 50 but modest, and the Day 30 sample size is not stated.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT on Days 2 to 6, AUT novelty and expert-rated solution creativity were higher (e.g., Day 6 AUT novelty 39.84 vs 14.80, t = -4.84, p < .001; Table 2a p. 8, Table 1 p. 11), but on Day 7 without ChatGPT differences were not significant (novelty p = 0.053; solution creativity p = 0.122), while SBERT similarity stayed higher in the ChatGPT group at Day 30 (0.39 vs 0.33, p <= .001; p. 14, Table 3 p. 16).
open_questions: Day 30 AUT novelty: Table 1 reports Estimate -3.69, p = 0.038 (significant), but the text (p. 7) says no significant difference, and the Table 2a means (2.40 vs 2.56) do not match the estimate. Day 30 usefulness has the same mismatch (5.62 vs 5.55 vs estimate -6.26).

Task 2 usefulness appears in Table 1 and Figure 2b but not in the methods' list of Task 2 ratings (p. 6); Day 7 usefulness is significant (p = 0.021) though the text says all Day 7 p-values were insignificant.

Diversity tests: the paper does not name the test or the unit behind 'ps <= .01' and 'p <= .001' for SBERT similarity; Table 3 and Table 2a notes refer to bold cells that do not exist. Whether pairs mix ideas from the same participant is not stated.
Text p. 15 gives Day 1 string-matching redundancy as 0.36 vs 0.35, which are the SBERT values; Table 3 shows 3.44 vs 3.51.
Number of tasks differs across the paper: 16 (p. 3), 14 (p. 4), 8 AUT + 7 product tasks (p. 24). Number of Day 30 respondents is not stated.
notes: Day 1 is a post-randomization, pre-treatment baseline with no AI in either arm; I recorded its numbers inside contrasts but not as outcomes. Table 1 Estimate = Control minus GPT (negative = GPT higher), verified against Table 2a/2b means. More than 15 outcomes: omitted Task 2 content quality Day 7 (Table 1: -0.41, -1.54, p 0.130; Table 2b 3.15 vs 3.56), public favor Days 2-6 (Table 1 Day 2 -1.28, -5.35; Day 3 -0.94, -3.89; Day 4 -0.99, -4.57; Day 5 -0.97, -3.69; Day 6 -1.44, -5.76; all p 0.000) and Day 7 (-0.25, -0.87, p 0.387), market success Days 2-6 (Day 2 -1.40, -5.47; Day 3 -0.91, -3.90; Day 4 -1.15, -5.21; Day 5 -1.00, -4.51; Day 6 -1.21, -5.57; all p 0.000) and Day 7 (-0.29, -1.03, p 0.308), and AUT self-recognition accuracy for novelty and usefulness (Judgement N/U; Table 1, Table 2a, appendix p. 28; mostly ns, Judgement N Day 3 1.03, p 0.010; Judgement U Day 6 0.62, p 0.008). String matching and UMAP density measures are folded into the SBERT outcomes as variants. Task 2 was not given at Day 30. Ideas: 3302 AUT ideas and 427 solutions in total (abstract), 351 to 501 ideas per day. Raters: two per task, blind to purpose and condition; Task 2 raters had new-project-development experience.
